idiom_name: intersection with a brand property that never exists at runtime
implementation_notes: TypeScript's structural typing means an empty interface matches every non-nullish value - the reason the no-empty-interface lint rule exists - so nominal marking is done with branded types: intersect the base type with an object carrying a brand property that never exists at run time. The brand makes structurally identical types mutually incompatible at compile time, and values are created by assertion at trusted boundaries. Nothing is enforced at run time, so validation must still happen where data enters.
pitfalls: Brands are compile-time only: as any, a cast, or a JSON round-trip erases the mark.
A string brand can be forged by any module that knows the property name; keep the brand key unexported when that matters.
Operations that reconstruct primitives (id + "", JSON.parse) lose the brand, so re-assert or validate at re-entry points.

variants.name: Unique symbol brand key
variants.idiom_name: declare const brand: unique symbol used as the brand key
variants.implementation_notes: A declare const brand: unique symbol used as the brand key keeps the mark out of the runtime shape and makes the key impossible to collide with, because the symbol never crosses a module boundary unless it is exported. This is the hardened form of the branded type: another module can copy a string brand but cannot produce an unexported unique symbol. The symbol does not exist at runtime unless emitted, so nothing is checked when the code runs.
pitfalls: If the unique symbol is exported, other modules can forge the brand; keep it module-private for closed categories.
Declarations that must appear in .d.ts files need the symbol declared alongside, or consumers cannot name the type.
Like all brands, the mark is erased at run time and survives only through disciplined assertions at boundaries.
